rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as the position, which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.
The answer explicitly provides the substance of the requirement by stating that Annex IV point 1(e) requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No, the AI system is not "medium risk", because the AI Act has no medium-risk category; under Article 6(1) it counts as high-risk. It meets the first condition because it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes the Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745 at point 11. It also meets the second condition because that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment before it is placed on the market. This holds whatever risk class the device has under the MDR and whether or not the AI system is placed on the market separately. References: Article 6(1); Annex I, point 11.
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that the AI Act has no medium-risk category and that the system is high-risk under Article 6(1).
The answer states the substance that the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, specifically citing the Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745.
The answer explicitly confirms that the product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, satisfying condition (b).
The answer explains that the classification under the AI Act is independent of the device's risk class under the MDR, capturing the cumulative and overriding nature of Article 6(1).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality while clearly conveying regulatory reasoning.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: The system is not prohibited and, on these facts, it is not high-risk. It is not prohibited because none of the practices in Article 5(1) covers it. The closest one, Article 5(1)(h), is limited to "real-time" remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. A one-to-one check that confirms a person's claimed identity is not identification. It is also not biometric categorisation under Article 5(1)(g). It is not high-risk under Article 6(2) because Annex III point 1(a) lists remote biometric identification systems but expressly excludes "AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be." That only holds while confirming identity is genuinely the system's sole purpose. The system would still be high-risk under Article 6(1) if it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I legislation that requires a third-party conformity assessment. References: Article 5(1); Article 6(1), (2); Annex III, point 1(a). Because Annex I includes products such as machinery, lifts, and equipment for explosive atmospheres, which may require such verification systems as safety components.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the system is not prohibited and explains why, including that it does not fall under Article 5(1)(h) or other prohibited practices.
The answer states the system is not high-risk under Article 6(2) due to the Annex III exclusion, and clarifies the condition for that exclusion, satisfying the substance of the criterion.

The answer directly references and applies the exclusion in Annex III.1(a) for biometric verification systems with the sole purpose of confirming identity, stating its applicability to the described system.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents reasoning in a logical, actionable manner for a compliance context.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 governs human oversight: high-risk AI systems must be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use (Article 14(1)). The measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and must be built in by the provider or identified by the provider for the deployer to implement (Article 14(3)). They must enable overseers to understand capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret output, disregard, override or reverse it, and interrupt the system through a "stop" button (Article 14(4)). For Annex III point 1(a) remote biometric identification systems, two natural persons must separately verify an identification before it is acted on, unless Union or national law considers this disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum (Article 14(5)). References: Article 14; Annex III, point 1(a). And asylum (Article 14(5)).
criteria_text: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that Article 14 governs human oversight.
The answer states that high-risk AI systems must be designed so natural persons can effectively oversee them during use.
The answer conveys that oversight aims to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights, particularly where risks persist despite other requirements.
The answer specifies that measures are either built in by the provider or identified by the provider for implementation by the deployer.

The answer lists the capabilities overseers must have: understanding capacities and limitations, monitoring operation, interpreting output, overriding or reversing output, and halting the system via a stop button.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.
criteria_text: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly acknowledges the existence of exceptions under Article 53(2).
The answer states the model must be released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution.
The answer specifies that parameters, including weights, architecture, and usage information, must be made publicly available.
The answer clearly limits the exception to points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), and explicitly excludes (c) and (d) from the exception.
The answer states that the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, which remain subject to full obligations.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a logical, actionable manner for a compliance audience.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Under Article 99(3), breaching the Article 5 prohibited AI practices can lead to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. This is the highest fine level in the Regulation, compared with EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % under Article 99(4) for other operator and notified-body obligations. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) applies the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount instead. References: Article 99(3), (4) and (6); Article 5.
criteria_text: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the fine amount as EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, which matches the substance of criterion 1.

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;
criteria_text: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person
criterion_remarks: The answer states that deep fakes are AI-generated or manipulated content, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies image, audio or video content, which matches the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the content resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response is concise, uses neutral and professional language consistent with regulatory definitions, and presents the information in a single, clear sentence suitable for a compliance context.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
criteria_text: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies high-risk systems under Article 6 and references both Annex I and Annex III, capturing the full substance of the criterion.
The answer states that limited-risk systems are subject to Article 50 transparency duties, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer acknowledges minimal or no risk systems are not subject to high-risk obligations and notes the availability of voluntary codes under Article 95, satisfying the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a coherent, regulatory-appropriate manner without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).
criteria_text: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, clearly affirming that a non-provider operator can be seen as a provider.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(a) by explaining that putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service triggers provider status.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(b) by describing substantial modification of a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk as a triggering action.

The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(c) by explaining that modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk AI system (including general-purpose) so that it becomes high-risk results in provider status.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Under Article 1(1), the objective of the EU AI Act is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI. At the same time, it must ensure a high level of protection against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union. That protection covers health, safety and the fundamental rights in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, while supporting innovation. References: Article 1(1).
criteria_text: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation
criterion_remarks: The answer states the objective to improve the functioning of the internal market.
The answer explicitly mentions promoting the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI.
The answer covers the high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights, including democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection, against harmful effects of AI systems.
The answer includes support for innovation as part of the objective.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).
criteria_text: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as its first word and maintains that position throughout, clearly aligning with the required verdict.

The answer explicitly states that structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task and that it falls under Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a), capturing the substance of the criterion.

The answer includes the condition that the derogation does not apply if the system profiles natural persons, stating 'the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons', which conveys the required exception.

The answer references Article 6(4) and states that the provider must document the assessment before market placement or putting into service, satisfying the requirement to state the substance of the obligation.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Under Article 101(5), the Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions that fix a fine on a provider of a general-purpose AI model. When it reviews such a decision, the Court may cancel, reduce or increase the fine. This applies to fines imposed under Article 101(1), which can be up to 3% of annual total worldwide turnover or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, where the provider intentionally or negligently breached the Regulation, failed to comply with information requests, measures or model-access requests, or supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information. References: Article 101(1); Article 101(5).
criteria_text: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine
criterion_remarks: The answer states the Court has 'unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions that fix a fine,' which conveys the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may cancel' the fine, satisfying the criterion.
The answer includes that the Court 'may reduce the fine,' which matches the criterion.
The answer states the Court 'may increase the fine,' directly reflecting the criterion.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: Information for registration in the EU database (Article 49 requires providers (and deployers that are public authorities) to register themselves and their high-risk AI system in the EU database (Article 71) before placing the system on the market or putting it into service.): Section A populated by provider / authorised representative (system name, intended purpose, components/datasets, design specifications, instructions for use, CE marking, conformity-assessment certificate, supervisory authority); Section B for Article 6(3) non-high-risk assessments; Section C populated by public-authority deployers. Public-access carve-out for law enforcement / migration / asylum / border-control systems. EU database for high-risk AI systems and GPAI models registered under Articles 49 + 60, set up and managed by the Commission, with public + restricted-access sections; data is machine-readable + navigable + searchable. Requires providers (and deployers that are public authorities) to register themselves and their high-risk AI system in the EU database (Article 71) before placing the system on the market or putting it into service.
criteria_text: Contact details of the provider, of any person submitting on its behalf and of the authorised representative, where applicable (Annex VIII, Section A, points 1 to 3)
AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (point 4)
Intended purpose and the components and functions the system supports (point 5)
Basic and concise description of the data and inputs used and the operating logic (point 6)
Market status and the notified body certificate details with a scanned copy, where applicable (points 7 to 9)
Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use (points 10 to 12)
criterion_remarks: The answer mentions 'system name' and 'supervisory authority' but does not explicitly state the contact details of the provider, any person submitting on its behalf, or the authorised representative, which are required by point 1 to 3.
While 'system name' is mentioned, the answer does not specify the need for an 'unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability' as required by point 4.
The answer refers to 'intended purpose' and 'components/datasets', but does not clearly state that the system's supported components and functions must be described as required in point 5.
While 'design specifications' and 'datasets' are mentioned, there is no explicit mention of a basic and concise description of the operating logic, which is required by point 6.

The answer references a 'conformity-assessment certificate' and implies market placement, but does not explicitly state the requirement to report the market status (point 7), nor does it mention the type, number, expiry date, notified body details, or scanned copy of the certificate (points 8–9).

The answer mentions 'instructions for use' but does not explicitly state submission of the EU declaration of conformity or list the Member States where the system is made available, which are required by points 10 to 12.

It also includes extraneous details about database management and public access, undermining clarity. rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.
criteria_text: Language: drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established
Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that the certificate must be drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State where the notified body is established, which matches the substance of criterion 1.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive
criterion_remarks: The answer states that processing is allowed only when strictly necessary for bias detection/correction and cannot be effectively achieved with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Under Article 13(3), the provider must supply instructions for use, in an appropriate digital format or otherwise, containing concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers (Article 13(2)). The required categories are: the identity and contact details of the provider and any authorised representative; the system's characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, namely its intended purpose, tested accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels and the circumstances affecting them, foreseeable circumstances creating health, safety or fundamental-rights risks, where applicable output-explanation capabilities, when appropriate performance on specific persons or groups and input or training-data specifications, and where applicable information for interpreting outputs; changes pre-determined at the initial conformity assessment; human-oversight measures, including technical measures that help interpret outputs; the computational and hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance, care and software-update measures; and, where relevant, the mechanisms for collecting, storing and interpreting logs. References: Article 13(2), Article 13(3).
criteria_text: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the instructions must include the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, the authorised representative.

The answer includes 'changes pre-determined at the initial conformity assessment' as a required category.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Under Article 95, codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both. Any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society organisations and academia, may be involved (Article 95(3)). The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of these codes, including related governance mechanisms. The codes are meant to foster voluntary application of some or all Chapter III, Section 2 requirements to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems (Article 95(1)). When doing so, the AI Office and the Member States must take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups (Article 95(4)). References: Article 95(1), (3) and (4). Taking into account the available technical solutions and industry best practices allowing for the application of such requirements.

May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1), a provider's quality management system for high-risk AI systems must be documented systematically in written policies, procedures and instructions, and include at least: a regulatory-compliance strategy covering conformity assessment and modification management; design, design-control and verification techniques; development, quality-control and quality-assurance techniques; examination, test and validation procedures; technical specifications, including standards; data-management systems and procedures; the risk management system; post-market monitoring; serious-incident reporting procedures; handling of communication with authorities, notified bodies and other parties; record-keeping systems; resource management, including security of supply; and an accountability framework for management and staff. Under Article 17(2), implementation may be scaled to the size of the provider's organisation, but it must still reach the rigour and level of protection the Regulation requires. Under Article 17(3), (4), providers with sectoral quality-management duties may build these elements into their existing system, and financial institutions meet the obligation through their internal-governance rules, except for the risk management system, post-market monitoring and incident reporting (points (g), (i)). References: Article 17.
criteria_text: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle

Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Under Article 5(1)(h), law enforcement may use "real-time" remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces only when this is strictly necessary for one of three objectives. These are: the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, and the search for missing persons; the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; and the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for a criminal investigation, prosecution or executing a criminal penalty. The third objective applies only to offences listed in Annex II that are punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order with a maximum of at least four years. Under Article 5(2), the use may only confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual. References: Article 5; Annex II.

Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order

The answer includes the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine terrorist attack threat, using substantively equivalent terms.
The answer specifies that the localisation or identification of a suspect applies only to Annex II offences punishable by at least four years’ custodial sentence or detention order.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Under Article 50(2), providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content, including general-purpose AI systems, must ensure that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and are detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Their technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as this is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. This duty does not apply to the extent that the system performs an assistive function for standard editing, does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. References: Article 50(2).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: Under Article 88(1), the Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, and it must entrust implementing these tasks to the AI Office. This applies without prejudice to the Commission's powers of organisation and to the division of competences between Member States and the Union under the Treaties, and it takes into account the procedural guarantees in Article 94. Under Article 88(2), national market surveillance authorities may ask the Commission to exercise these powers where necessary and proportionate to help them carry out their tasks under the Regulation, without prejudice to Article 75(3). References: Article 88(1); Article 88(2).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Under Article 60(4)(e), data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions may be transferred to third countries only if appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented. This is one of the cumulative conditions in Article 60(4) that must all be met before any real-world testing outside an AI regulatory sandbox can take place. The Act does not list the safeguards itself; it relies on existing Union law, mainly the GDPR's rules on international transfers for personal data, with extra protection for special categories of data under GDPR Article 9. References: Article 60(4)(e).

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions do not all need to be met at once: under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as having systemic risk if it meets any of the alternative conditions. Under Article 51(1)(a), the model has high-impact capabilities, assessed with appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks. Article 51(2) presumes this when the cumulative compute used for training is greater than 10^25 floating-point operations. Alternatively, under Article 51(1)(b), the Commission decides that the model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those high-impact capabilities, having regard to the Annex XIII criteria. The Commission can make that decision on its own initiative (ex officio) or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel. References: Article 51; Annex XIII.

No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No, it is not automatically high-risk under Article 6(1). It meets the first condition, because the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, namely the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (Annex I, point 11). It fails the second condition in Article 6(1)(b): that product must be "required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment", and a Class I device that is not sterile, does not measure and is not a reusable surgical instrument is normally self-declared by its manufacturer without a notified body, so the system is not high-risk on this route unless it also falls under an Annex III use case. References: Article 6(1); Annex I, point 11.

Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes, it can. Under Article 6(1), an AI system used as a safety component in a lift is high-risk, whether it is placed on the market or put into service on its own or together with the lift. Two conditions must both be met. The AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I. Lifts fall under this because Annex I, point 4 lists Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts and safety components for lifts. Under that Directive, the lift or safety component in question must undergo a third-party conformity assessment before it is placed on the market or put into service. If no third-party assessment is required, the system is not high-risk through this route. References: Article 6(1); Annex I, point 4.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Under Article 20(2), a provider that becomes aware that its high-risk AI system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) must immediately investigate the causes itself. Where applicable, it does this together with the deployer that reported the risk. It must also inform the competent market surveillance authorities, and where applicable the notified body, of the nature of the non-compliance and of any corrective action taken. Article 20(1) separately requires the provider to take corrective action immediately where it considers, or has reason to consider, that the system is not in conformity: bring it into conformity, withdraw it, disable it or recall it, as appropriate. The authority's own evaluation under Article 79(2) runs alongside the provider's investigation and does not replace it, and the provider must cooperate with it. References: Article 20; Article 79.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate. Article 24(3) says that distributors "shall ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the compliance of the system with the requirements set out in Section 2." The words "where applicable" cover the operator's point: if you only deliver software, the duty may have little to apply to, but a high-risk AI system can also come as hardware or as part of a physical product, and damage in storage or transit could affect compliance. Note that the duty is limited to the time the system is under the operator's responsibility, and the condition it must protect is compliance with the Section 2 requirements. References: Article 24(3).

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: The AI Act doesn't ban or regulate drones as such. Whether drone AI is prohibited or high-risk depends on what the AI is used for (Article 5, Article 6). Using AI to identify people around town is remote biometric identification. Article 5(1)(h) prohibits it only when it is real-time, in publicly accessible spaces, and used for law enforcement, unless it is strictly necessary for one of three purposes: searching for specific abduction, trafficking or sexual-exploitation victims or missing persons; preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or a terrorist attack; or locating or identifying suspects of Annex II offences punishable by at least four years. Any other remote biometric identification by a drone, including post-event or private use, is high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III point 1(a), where Union or national law permits it. A toy drone's AI is high-risk under Article 6(1) only if the AI is a safety component of the toy, or is itself the product, under the Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC (an Annex I law), and the toy needs a third-party conformity assessment. If a toy drone is used for a listed Annex III purpose, such as identifying people, it is high-risk no matter what kind of product it is. References: Article 5(1)(h); Article 6(1), (2); Annex III point 1(a). Unless it falls under the permitted exceptions outlined in Article 5(1)(h).

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply go ahead: the system remains a high-risk AI system, and the operator must keep its logs for the new use. As a deployer, Article 26(1) requires the operator to use it in accordance with its instructions for use, and a use outside the intended purpose departs from those instructions. The operator's legal team's finding that no Annex I or Annex III case applies only means the new use would not make a system high-risk on its own under Article 6(1) or 6(2). It does not remove the high-risk classification the system already has. Article 25(1)(c) is not triggered, because it only applies where someone changes the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk. However, if the repurposing amounts to a substantial modification, Article 25(1) would make you the provider, with all provider obligations. Under Article 26(6), the operator must keep the logs the system automatically generates, to the extent they are under the operator's control, for at least six months unless Union or national law, in particular data-protection law, provides otherwise. References: Article 26(1), (6); Article 6(1), (2); Article 25(1).

Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes, it can be high-risk under Article 6(1), read with Annex I, point 11. Software intended to support treatment decisions is typically a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR). Article 6(1) makes such a system high-risk when two conditions are both met. First, it is the product itself, or a safety component of a product, covered by the MDR. Second, the MDR requires that product to undergo a third-party conformity assessment before it is placed on the market or put into service. In practice, MDR Rule 11 places decision-support software in class IIa or higher, which requires a notified body. Annex III does not list clinical treatment support as a use case, so this is a product route rather than a listed-use route. The Article 6(3) derogation only applies to Annex III systems, so it cannot remove the high-risk status here. References: Article 6(1); Annex I, point 11.

Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Under Article 53(1)(b) and Annex XII, the operator must disclose the first four items to downstream providers, but not samples of outlier data. Here is each item. Date of release: yes. Annex XII, point 1(c) requires "the date of release and methods of distribution". Number of parameters: yes. Annex XII, point 1(f) requires "the architecture and number of parameters". How the model interacts with hardware: yes, where applicable. Annex XII, point 1(d) requires a description of how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself. Licence: yes. Annex XII, point 1(h) requires "the licence for the model". Samples of outlier data used in training: no. Annex XII, point 2(c) requires only information on the training, testing and validation data, where applicable: the type and provenance of the data and the curation methods. It does not require the data or samples of it. This duty does not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, unless the model has systemic risk (Article 53(2)). Disclosure is also without prejudice to protecting intellectual property, confidential business information and trade secrets (Article 53(1)(b)). References: Article 53(1)(b); Article 53(2); Annex XII.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, healthcare decision-making is not a separate area in Annex III, which lists eight high-risk areas under Article 6(2): biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Healthcare falls only under specific use-cases in Annex III point 5: public authorities assessing eligibility for healthcare services (5(a)), risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance (5(c)), and emergency healthcare patient triage (5(d)). Clinical decision-support AI is high-risk under Article 6(1) instead when it is a medical device, or a safety component of one, under MDR/IVDR (Annex I) that requires third-party conformity assessment. References: Article 6; Annex III.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Adding guardrails does not move an agentic system out of the high-risk category, but changing its intended purpose can. The Act has no "moderate risk" tier. Under Article 6, high-risk status depends on two things: whether the system is a safety component or product under Annex I legislation that needs third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)), or whether its intended purpose matches a use-case listed in Annex III (Article 6(2)). How much risk is left after mitigation does not change that classification. Guardrails are risk-control measures that a high-risk system must already have under Article 9. Changing capabilities and intended purpose can remove the classification, either by moving the system outside every Annex III use-case or by fitting it into the Article 6(3) exception. That exception needs no significant risk of harm plus one of four conditions: a narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or a preparatory task. A system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk, and the provider must document this assessment before placing the system on the market. Going the other way, anyone who changes a non-high-risk system's intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk is treated as its provider under Article 25(1)(c). References: Article 6; Article 9; Article 25(1)(c).

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is allowed, but Article 50(4) requires disclosure if the images count as deep fakes. In that case, the university as deployer must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, and the Act gives no exemption for educational or illustrative use. The lighter regime, where disclosure only has to avoid hampering the display or enjoyment of the work, covers only evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, and the Act does not say whether teaching illustrations count as "analogous". The law-enforcement exception does not apply here, and it is not a lighter regime anyway: it removes the duty entirely, but only for uses authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. References: Article 50(4).

Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No, this system is not high-risk. Under Article 6(2), a system is high-risk only if it falls within a use case listed in Annex III. The retailer's comparison to policing points to Annex III, point 6 (law enforcement), but every use case in point 6 requires the system to be used "by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities", or by Union institutions in support of them. A supermarket flagging transactions for its own staff does not meet that condition. Because the tool uses no biometrics, Annex III, point 1 does not apply either. The practice is also not prohibited under Article 5(1). Point (c) does not apply because the tool builds no social score over time, and no treatment follows in unrelated contexts. Point (d) does not apply because the risk flag comes from objective current-transaction anomalies, not "solely on the profiling of a natural person or on assessing their personality traits", and staff make the final decision. References: Article 6(2); Annex III, point 6; Article 5(1).
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, this system is not high-risk,' which matches the required verdict.

The answer explicitly states that every use case in Annex III.6 requires use 'by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities' or by Union institutions in support of them, conveying the substance of the criterion.

The answer directly explains that a supermarket flagging transactions for its own staff does not meet the 'by or on behalf of law enforcement' condition, thus clearly stating the reasoning in the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with logical structure and no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, you cannot skip the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. Under Article 43(3), those requirements apply to high-risk AI systems covered by Section A of Annex I and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment. Using the sectoral opt-out does not change this, for two reasons: the system remains high-risk under Article 6(1) because its product falls under Annex I legislation that requires third-party conformity assessment, and Article 43(3) lets you use the opt-out only if you have also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements. References: Article 6(1); Article 43(3).
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot skip the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements,' which matches the required verdict of 'No' in criterion 1.
The answer states that Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment, citing Article 43(3), second sentence, which conveys the substance of the criterion.
The answer explains that the opt-out is available only if harmonised standards or common specifications cover all Section 2 requirements, directly reflecting the condition in the third criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents a logical flow suitable for regulatory advice.
